Moreover butterflies are especially useful when dealing with habitat fragmentation as many species operate as metapopulations (Brückmann et al. 2010). Therefore as a second step, we will study the constitution of species assemblages at park level using nestedness analysis. The concept of nestedness dates from the first half of the 20th century (Hulten 1937), and was first proposed to describe patterns of species composition for insular fauna (Darlington 1957). Nested patterns constitute typical patterns of fragmented landscape where assemblages of species-poor sites are subsets of species assemblages of more diverse sites (Patterson and Atmar 1986; Patterson 1987). Habitat fragmentation is known to be a major feature of urban areas (McKinney 2002), and is expected to generate nestedness in species assemblages as fragmented landscapes are characterized by patches that differ in size and relative isolation (Ulrich 2009; Patterson and Atmar 2000). Initially, two mechanisms were invoked to explain nested patterns among species assemblages: ordered sequences of colonization (Darlington 1957; Simberloff and Wilson 1969) and ordered sequences of extinction (Patterson and Atmar 1986; Patterson 1987). More recently, nestedness analysis has become increasingly popular (e.g., Wright et al. 1998; Fischer and Lindenmayer 2002; Almeida-Neto et al. 2008; Driscoll 2008; Ulrich et al. 2009) as it represents a useful tool to describe patterns of species occurrence, their underlying mechanisms and thus gradients that structure ecological communities (Ulrich 2009). Different processes can in fact lead to nested patterns in community structure: (i) extinction, (ii) colonization, and also (iii) disturbance, (iv) habitat distribution, (v) hierarchical niche relationships and (vi) passive sampling (Patterson and Atmar 2000). These potential causes of nested patterns have been extensively discussed (e.g., Cutler 1994; Driscoll 2008; Ulrich et al. 2009). Thus, nestedness analysis seems to be a suitable tool for understanding gradients structuring the composition of urban species assemblages.

Recorded species were characterised following the functional classification of Kitahara and Fujii (1994, 1997). On the basis of resource utilisation patterns by species, these authors proposed a classification according to 2 fundamental niche dimensions (time and food). Applying the generalist/ specialist concept to the analysis of butterfly community structure, they classified butterfly species based on 2 representative traits: larval resource breadth (range of host-plant species used by larvae) and voltinism (number of generations per year). They considered host-plant specificity as an indicator of the niche breadth in a larval food dimension, while the notion of voltinism was extended to serve as a surrogate for the niche breadth in a seasonal time dimension (see Kitahara and Fujii 1994, 1997). This classification resulted in 4 functional groups: (i) typical specialists (TS) which are uni- or bivoltine species that feed on host-plants belonging to 1 plant family only; (ii) typical generalists (TG) which are multivoltine species (3 generations or more per year) that feed on hostplants belonging to 2 or more plant families; (iii) rebound specialists (RS) which are multivoltine species that feed on host-plants belonging to 1 plant family only; and selective generalists (SeG) which are uni- or bivoltine species that feed on host-plants belonging to 2 or more plant families (see Online Resource 1) (Santin 2004; Lafranchis 2000; Tolman and Lewington 1999).

A total of 11 environmental variables have been used in order to characterize each of the 132 transects. They correspond to three different matrices representing three environmental scales: landscape scale (5 variables), park scale (4 variables) and sampling plot scale (2 variables).

As a first step, stepwise selections were performed, within each of the three groups of environmental variables, to exclude variables that did not contribute significantly to the explained variation in the 4 response variables (and thus to avoid saturated global model) . Thus, we performed a first series of (partial) regression analyses using redundancy analysis (RDA) and we selected variables within each group on the basis of Akaike information criterion (AIC) (Akaike 1978). We tested, for each environmental variable, both linear and quadratic terms. For each of the three sets of environmental variables (plot, park, landscape), the combination minimising the Akaike criterion was used to select the variables to include in the analysis. Note that for abundance of uni-bivoltine butterflies, analyses were performed on the 93 sampling plots where uni-bivoltine species occurred.

Nestedness analysis was performed on a presence-absence matrix with sites in columns and species in rows. The first step in nestedness analysis is the calculation of one or several metrics to quantify the pattern of nestedness in the matrix (Ulrich et al. 2009). Hence, to test whether the species composition of parks exhibited nestedness, we used 3 different metrics: (i) the discrepancy measure, BR (Brualdi and Sanderson 1999); (ii) the nestedness measure based on overlap and decreasing fill, NODF (Almeida-Neto et al. 2008) and (iii) the matrix temperature, T (Atmar and Patterson 1993). Both BR and NODF are interesting metrics as they combine various desired statistical properties: they are invariant to matrix size, shape and fill, the do not treat differentially presences and absences, and they are invariant to matrix transposition (Ulrich 2009). Although, T is positively correlated with matrix size (Ulrich and Gotelli 2007), it was also calculated as it remains to date the most widely used metric to assess nestedness (Atmar and Patterson 1993; Ulrich 2009). Here, we began without any assumption on gradient influencing the degree of nestedness. So the matrix was sorted according to row and column totals (i.e., parks were ordered from the richest to the poorest in terms of species richness, and species were ordered from the most frequent to the rarest). Metrics were then calculated for this packed matrix (see Online Resource 3).
